rationale:
Evidence: iteration 3 (score 685.6, best so far) used five 16 mm sensors at x = -0.03 to +0.03 m, weights [-2,-1,0,1,2], kp 4.0, kd 1.0, base_speed 1.5, mass 0.6 kg. It finished the oval 20/20 and the s-bend 17/20. Slalom still never finishes (0/20, progress 0.585, max_error 0.065, 1.25 line-loss events), so every slalom run leaves the track. Iteration 4 (score 342.7) widened the array to seven sensors and raised kp to 6.0. That collapsed the oval to 9/20 and the s-bend to 0/20, so the higher kp is the likely cause, and I am not going to repeat that combination. Body width cannot widen the off-track limit because the 0.06 m floor binds.

Change: from the iteration 3 design, reduce mass from 0.6 to 0.45 kg and keep everything else fixed (five sensors, weights, kp 4.0, kd 1.0, base_speed 1.5, line_loss last_direction). Iteration 1 to 3 showed that the mass and kd change reduced slalom max_error and line loss while the oval and s-bend improved. Lower mass reduces yaw inertia, so the robot should correct sharp slalom bends faster. This is a single-variable change, so the effect on slalom can be read cleanly. Expected result: slalom max_error falls toward 0.06 or below, slalom progress rises above 0.6, and the oval stays near 100%. Hypotheses: (a) mass 0.45 cuts slalom line-loss events below 1.0; (b) the oval and s-bend completion holds; (c) steering_oscillation stays at or below about 0.35. If slalom still fails, the next step is a sensor lead (y toward 0.06 m) or a small kd increase, not kp.
